title: Musk’s Merger Math: More Control, No Trillion-Dollar Windfall
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

A potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla could give Elon Musk something more consequential than a trillion-dollar payout: majority voting control over the combined business.

According to Reuters, the distinction stems from how the companies structure his compensation. SpaceX gives Musk voting rights attached to certain stock awards before he earns their economic value. Tesla links additional stock and control to achieving operational and market-value milestones.

Barclays estimates that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla, at current valuations, could leave Musk owning approximately 37% of the combined company while controlling 56% of its votes. Some SpaceX shares carry ten votes apiece, creating that gap between ownership and influence.

A merger would not automatically unlock Tesla’s entire compensation package. Its change-of-control provisions could remove operational requirements, but valuation thresholds would still matter. Reuters reports that Tesla would need to reach at least $2 trillion for any awards under the plan. SpaceX’s board could also revise its compensation arrangements following a transaction. investing.com

The central implication is that financial rewards and corporate authority can follow different paths.

For investors, this raises a broader governance question: how much decision-making power should accompany each dollar of economic exposure? A shareholder can participate substantially in financial outcomes while having comparatively limited influence over strategy, directors or future transactions.

The proposed combination should therefore be assessed through two separate lenses. One concerns the industrial rationale: whether shared resources, technology and investment priorities would improve business performance. The other concerns accountability: whether shareholders would retain meaningful mechanisms to challenge decisions.

Those questions remain relevant regardless of the size of any eventual compensation award. An enormous headline pay figure attracts attention, but voting arrangements determine who can shape the company after a transaction closes. For shareholders evaluating a possible deal, understanding that distinction is essential to judging its lasting consequences.

Reuters: “Musk’s pay under a SpaceX–Tesla merger: voting control, but no $1 trillion payday” — Chris Kirkham, November 3, 2026.
